original_content.knowledge_point: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating
original_content.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $(\frac{1}{xy}-\frac{1}{x})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
original_content.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{xy}-\frac{1}{x})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ \frac{1}{x}(\frac{1}{y}-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ (\frac{1}{y}-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \int (\frac{1}{y}-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y|-y & ={x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|-1 & ={1}^{2}+C \\ 0-1 & =1+C \\ C & =-2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $(\frac{1}{xy}-\frac{1}{x})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ in implicit form is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|-y={x}^{2}-2\,.
$$

corrected_content.knowledge_point: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating
corrected_content.problem: Determine whether a differentiable classical solution on an open interval containing the initial point exists for the differential equation $(\frac{1}{xy}-\frac{1}{x})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
corrected_content.worked_solution:
A classical solution must be differentiable on an interval containing $x=1$ and satisfy the differential equation at that point. Substituting $x=1$ and $y(1)=1$ gives

$$\left(\frac{1}{1\cdot1}-\frac11\right)y'(1)=2,\qquad 0\cdot y'(1)=2.$$

This is impossible for a finite derivative. Therefore no differentiable classical solution exists for the stated initial condition.

Formal separation on nonsingular regions gives

$$(1/y-1)\,dy=2x\,dx,\qquad \ln|y|-y=x^2+C.$$

Requiring the integrated level set to contain $(1,1)$ yields $C=-2$, hence $\ln|y|-y=x^2-2$. This is the source's formally integrated relation, but it is not a classical solution of the IVP. Differentiating it at $(1,1)$ again requires $0\cdot y'(1)=2$. Near $y=1$, continuity would give $y>0$, and $\ln y-y\le -1$ makes $x^2\le1$ necessary on that level set, so it cannot supply a graph on a two-sided neighborhood of $x=1$ either.

The source capture and its accepted formal relation are retained for provenance. The corrected study answer concerns the original IVP's existence.
